title: Pokémon
text:
Pokémon is a Japanese media franchise owned and managed by The Pokémon Company, a joint venture between Nintendo Co., Ltd., Game Freak Inc., and Creatures Inc., centered on fictional creatures known as Pokémon that are captured, trained, and battled by humans called trainers in a shared universe. The franchise debuted in 1996 with the role-playing video games Pokémon Red and Pokémon Green for the Game Boy, developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo exclusively in Japan before expanding internationally in 1998 as Pokémon Red and Blue. Created by Satoshi Tajiri, who drew inspiration from his childhood hobby of collecting insects, Pokémon has grown into a multimedia phenomenon encompassing video games, an animated television series, films, a trading card game, manga, and merchandise.

The core video game series, which follows a generational release pattern tied to Nintendo consoles, has sold over 495 million units worldwide as of November 2025, making it one of the best-selling video game franchises ever. Key titles include the original Generation I games (1996), which introduced 151 Pokémon species, up to Generation IX's Pokémon Scarlet and Violet (2022) and their expansions, bringing the total number of distinct Pokémon species to 1,025 as documented in the official National Pokédex. Spin-off games like Pokémon GO (2016), an augmented reality mobile title developed with Niantic, revolutionized interactive entertainment by encouraging real-world exploration and achieved over 1 billion downloads globally. Pokémon Legends: Z-A (2025), released on October 16 for Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 systems and selling over 5.8 million units, explores the Kalos region with a focus on urban redevelopment and Mega Evolutions.

Beyond games, the Pokémon anime series premiered in Japan on April 1, 1997, and has broadcast over 1,200 episodes across more than 25 seasons in over 190 countries as of 2025, following protagonists like Ash Ketchum (until 2023) and now the rising trainers Liko and Roy in Pokémon Horizons: The Series. The franchise includes 23 animated feature films released between 1998 and 2020, with the latest being Pokémon the Movie: Secrets of the Jungle. The Pokémon Trading Card Game, launched in 1996 in Japan and 1999 internationally, has produced over 75 billion cards by March 2025, supporting competitive play through annual World Championships. Manga adaptations, such as Pokémon Adventures, have sold tens of millions of copies, while merchandise ranges from toys and apparel to theme park attractions like Pokémon Centers in Japan and collaborations worldwide.

Pokémon's global impact is profound, recognized as the highest-grossing media franchise in history with lifetime revenues exceeding $147 billion as of 2024, surpassing properties like Hello Kitty and Star Wars through diversified revenue streams including $102.9 billion from merchandise and licensing alone. It has fostered a dedicated fan community, annual events like Pokémon Day (February 27), and esports tournaments, while promoting themes of friendship, exploration, and environmental awareness. Despite challenges like market saturation, the franchise continues to innovate, with recent releases like the chibi-style short anime series Monpoké (2025) and upcoming titles including the life simulation game Pokémon Pokopia (2026).

#Overview

#Name and Etymology

The term "Pokémon" is a portmanteau derived from the Japanese katakana words poketto (ポケット, from English "pocket") and monsutā (モンスター, from English "monster"), reflecting the franchise's central idea of capturing and containing fantastical creatures within compact, portable Poké Balls. This linguistic blend emerged during the development of the original video games by Game Freak, where the full title in Japanese was Pocket Monsters (ポケットモンスター, Poketto Monsutā), emphasizing the small-scale portability of the monsters.

The etymology of the name traces back to creator Satoshi Tajiri's personal experiences as a child in rural Machida, near Tokyo, where he passionately collected insects, trapping them in small cases to study and trade with friends. Tajiri, who grew up in the 1970s amid urban development that diminished natural habitats for bug hunting, sought to evoke the thrill of exploration and collection in Pokémon, allowing players—especially city-dwelling children—to virtually "catch" and manage creatures as he once did with beetles and butterflies. This inspiration transformed his hobby into a core thematic element, with the "pocket" aspect underscoring the accessibility of such adventures via handheld devices like the Game Boy.

Initially released in Japan in 1996 under the full Pocket Monsters title, the franchise's branding evolved for international audiences with the 1998 North American launch of Pokémon Red and Blue, where the abbreviated "Pokémon" was adopted as the primary English name to streamline global recognition and marketing. This shift retained the Japanese shorthand while establishing "Pokémon" as a standalone brand identity, influencing its entry into English dictionaries and widespread cultural use. Accompanying this branding, the official English tagline "Pokémon: Gotta Catch 'em All!" was introduced, encapsulating the core gameplay mechanic of capturing all available Pokémon species.

Nintendo and its partners began registering trademarks for "Pokémon" in Japan as early as September 1995, with the inaugural filing for Pocket Monsters by Creatures Inc., ahead of the games' debut. Following the formation of The Pokémon Company in 1998 as a joint venture between Nintendo, Game Freak, and Creatures, the entity expanded trademark protections internationally across categories like video games, merchandise, and media, securing registrations in the United States by 2001.

#Core Gameplay and Concepts

The Pokémon franchise revolves around players assuming the role of Pokémon Trainers in a fictional world inhabited by diverse creatures called Pokémon, where the core objective is to capture, train, and battle these beings across expansive regions modeled after real-world locales, such as Kanto, which is inspired by Japan's Kantō region including elements from creator Satoshi Tajiri's hometown of Machida. Trainers embark on journeys to explore these regions, forming bonds with Pokémon while navigating environments like forests, caves, and cities teeming with wild Pokémon and other trainers. Central to the experience is the Pokédex, a high-tech encyclopedia provided by regional Pokémon Professors—scholarly figures who study Pokémon biology and distribute starter Pokémon to new trainers, such as Grass-type Turtwig, Fire-type Chimchar, or Water-type Piplup in the Sinnoh region.

Core mechanics emphasize strategic turn-based battles, where trainers command up to six Pokémon per team to engage opponents using a moveset of up to four attacks at a time, depleting the foe's Hit Points (HP) until they reach zero and faint, a mechanic designed to portray exhaustion rather than death for a family-friendly tone. Capturing wild Pokémon involves weakening them in battle and throwing a Poké Ball to encase and convert them to the trainer's team, with success influenced by the target's HP, status conditions, and ball type; once caught, Pokémon can be trained through battles to gain experience and levels, enabling evolution into stronger forms via leveling, items like Fire Stones, or trading. Battles hinge on an 18-type system—including Normal, Fire, Water, Electric, Grass, Ice, Fighting, Poison, Ground, Flying, Psychic, Bug, Rock, Ghost, Dragon, Dark, Steel, and Fairy—where each type has advantages (super effective, dealing 2x damage), disadvantages (not very effective, 0.5x damage), or immunities (0x damage), as charted in official type compatibility guides to encourage tactical team composition.

The Pokémon world is structured around progression challenges, including battles against Gym Leaders—elite trainers in specialized arenas who focus on one or two types and guard badges symbolizing mastery—to qualify for the Pokémon League, the pinnacle tournament where victors confront the Elite Four, a quartet of formidable specialists, followed by the regional Champion. This framework fosters exploration and rivalry, with no permanent harm to Pokémon, as fainted ones recover at Pokémon Centers run by helpful Nurses Joy. Lore enriches the universe through over 1,025 distinct species by November 2025, each featuring unique designs, innate abilities (passive effects like Levitate for immunity to Ground moves), and Pokédex entries detailing habitats, behaviors, and fictional biology, such as Pikachu's electric cheek pouches or Bulbasaur's symbiotic seed bulb. Among them, Legendary and Mythical Pokémon stand out as exceptionally rare, powerful entities often central to regional myths—Legendaries like the creation deity Arceus or guardian Zygarde embody cosmic or ecological roles, while Mythicals like the elusive Mew represent hidden origins—typically encountered singly and restricted in competitive play due to their overwhelming strength.

#History

#Origins and Early Development

Satoshi Tajiri, born in 1965 in Setagaya, Tokyo, developed a passion for insect collecting during his childhood in rural Machida, where he and his friends would explore forests and trade their catches. As urbanization encroached on these natural areas in the 1970s and 1980s, making rare insects harder to find, Tajiri sought ways to preserve and share this joy of discovery. In 1989, inspired by his interest in video games, he founded Game Freak as a fanzine to share arcade tips and strategies with fellow enthusiasts. This publication evolved into a game development studio, with its first project being the 1990 puzzle game Quinty (released internationally as Mendel Palace), a Famicom title developed by a small team using homemade tools on hacked NES hardware.

The concept for what would become Pokémon emerged in 1990 from Tajiri's desire to digitize the thrill of collecting and trading insects, initially pitched to Nintendo as Capsule Monsters. This early prototype envisioned players capturing and exchanging creatures stored in capsules, drawing directly from Tajiri's experiences of trading bugs with friends to foster connections among players. The name later evolved into "Pocket Monsters," reflecting the portable capsules and Game Boy hardware, emphasizing a world where children could virtually explore and share rarities lost to urban development.

Key collaborators on the project included Ken Sugimori, who served as art director and designed many of the initial creatures, such as early concepts for Rhydon and Nidoking, and Junichi Masuda, who handled music composition, sound programming, and overall audio development using a custom "Sound Driver" tool. Nintendo became involved in 1994 after reviewing the pitch, with Shigeru Miyamoto joining as producer to expand the game's scope, including increasing memory capacity to accommodate 151 Pokémon designs. Development of the Red and Green prototypes spanned from 1990 to 1995, conducted by a small team of about five members operating informally like a college club, focusing on core mechanics such as battling and trading via the Game Boy's link cable to enable real-time exchanges between players.

#Launch and Growth in Japan

The Pokémon video games Red and Green were released in Japan on February 27, 1996, for the Nintendo Game Boy, marking the franchise's debut as an RPG centered on collecting and battling creatures. Initial sales were modest but grew, with over one million units of Red, Green, and the enhanced Blue version sold in 1996, though the games featured Pikachu prominently as an early mascot in promotional materials to appeal to younger audiences. Marketing efforts emphasized interactive elements like trading via the Game Link Cable, and Pikachu's cute design helped build early buzz despite the limited initial production run.

To boost engagement, the franchise tied into CoroCoro Comic, where a manga adaptation titled Pocket Monsters began serialization in March 1996, introducing the world and characters to magazine readers through serialized adventures. A key promotional event was a lottery organized by CoroCoro in April 1996, offering 20 players the exclusive opportunity to receive the mythical Pokémon Mew via mail-order cartridge modification, marking the first in-game event distribution and generating excitement among fans. Later that year, an enhanced version, Pokémon Blue, launched on October 15, 1996, exclusively through mail-order for CoroCoro subscribers, incorporating updated graphics and Pokémon from both prior versions to encourage trading.

The franchise expanded further with the launch of the Pokémon Trading Card Game on October 20, 1996, published by Media Factory and developed by Creatures Inc., which adapted the core collection and battling mechanics into a collectible format with starter packs and booster sets. In early 1997, production of an anime adaptation was announced, leading to its premiere on TV Tokyo on April 1, 1997, which further popularized the characters and storyline among children. This version, Pokémon Yellow: Special Pikachu Edition, followed in September 1998 as an anime-inspired update to the original games, allowing players to start with Pikachu as their partner and incorporating elements like team dynamics from the show.

Growth faced significant challenges in 1997, particularly with the airing of the episode "Dennō Senshi Porygon" on December 16, which featured rapid flashing red and blue lights during a scene involving Pikachu's attack, triggering photosensitive epileptic seizures in 685 children across Japan, with 310 boys and 375 girls hospitalized. The incident prompted a four-month hiatus in anime production and the implementation of epilepsy warnings at the start of subsequent episodes, along with stricter guidelines for visual effects in Japanese television. Amid rising popularity and concerns over unauthorized merchandise, Tsunekazu Ishihara formed the Pokémon Copyright Council in 1997 to coordinate intellectual property protection, meeting weekly to oversee events, publications, and licensing across Nintendo, Creatures, and Game Freak.

#International Expansion

The Pokémon franchise entered the North American market with the release of Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue on September 28, 1998, published by Nintendo of America for the Game Boy. Originally titled Pocket Monsters in Japan, the series was rebranded as Pokémon internationally—a portmanteau of "pocket" and "monsters"—to evoke portability on the Game Boy while mitigating potential negative associations with the term "monster" in Western audiences. The launch was supported by a marketing campaign emphasizing collection and trading, leading to strong initial sales; by the end of 1999, the games had sold over 9 million copies in North America, contributing significantly to the franchise's global momentum.

Expansion continued into Europe and other regions in 1999, with Pokémon Red and Blue releasing on October 5 in much of Europe, adapted with localized titles such as Pokémon Rouge et Bleu in French-speaking markets and Pokémon Rot und Blau in German. Localization teams made targeted adjustments for cultural sensitivities, including redesigning the Pokémon Jynx—whose original black-skinned appearance evoked minstrel show stereotypes—by changing its color to purple in subsequent international releases starting with Pokémon Gold and Silver. These efforts ensured broader appeal while preserving core gameplay elements derived from Japanese origins.

Parallel to the games, international media adaptations accelerated the franchise's reach. The English-dubbed anime premiered in U.S. syndication on September 7, 1998, before shifting to the Kids' WB network on February 13, 1999, with 4Kids Entertainment handling dubbing and initial merchandising licensing. The Pokémon Trading Card Game followed suit, launching globally under Wizards of the Coast with the English Base Set on January 9, 1999, which quickly became a bestseller and integrated trading mechanics into Western markets.

Key milestones included the 2000 international release of Pokémon Gold and Silver on October 15 in North America—following their Japanese debut in November 1999—which introduced the Johto region, day-night cycles, and 100 new Pokémon species. Pikachu solidified its role as the franchise's universal mascot during this period, its cute design transcending cultural barriers and anchoring promotional efforts worldwide.

#Peak Popularity and Challenges

The phenomenon known as Pokémania reached its zenith in the United States during 1999 and 2000, fueled by the international launch of the video games and accompanying media. The Pokémon Trading Card Game (TCG), released in North America in January 1999, quickly dominated the market, generating approximately $568 million in sales for distributor Hasbro in 2000 alone and accounting for 15% of the company's total revenues that year. Video game sales also surged, with the original titles (Red, Blue, Yellow, and their Japanese counterparts) contributing to annual franchise revenues of nearly ¥400 billion (about $3.28 billion) by March 1999. This boom was supported by the establishment of Pokémon USA, Inc. in February 2001 (now part of The Pokémon Company International), which handled licensing in the Americas, and the rebranding of Japan's Pokémon Center Co., Ltd. to The Pokémon Company in October 2000 for centralized global management.

Key releases amplified the hype, including Pokémon Stadium for Nintendo 64, which debuted in Japan on April 30, 1999, and introduced 3D battles compatible with Game Boy titles via the Transfer Pak accessory. The first Pokémon film, Pokémon: The First Movie – Mewtwo Strikes Back, premiered in Japan on July 18, 1998, and in international markets starting November 10, 1999, grossing $163.6 million worldwide and becoming one of the highest-earning anime films at the time. These milestones solidified Pokémon's cultural grip, with merchandise and media tie-ins driving widespread enthusiasm among children.

However, the rapid rise led to significant challenges, including controversies over the TCG's addictive trading mechanics. In 1999, a class-action lawsuit in San Diego accused Nintendo of promoting illegal gambling through the cards, likening the collecting frenzy to lotteries and highlighting risks of obsession among youth. By 2000, numerous U.S. and U.K. schools imposed bans on Pokémon cards due to disruptions from trading disputes and playground fights, with administrators reporting sidelined classrooms and heightened conflicts. Market saturation exacerbated issues, culminating in a sharp sales dip for the TCG by early 2001, as the card market virtually collapsed and collectors faced devalued holdings. Additionally, performer Uri Geller filed a lawsuit in November 2000 against Nintendo, alleging that the Pokémon character Kadabra appropriated his likeness and spoon-bending persona, leading to the character's temporary removal from merchandise.

The anime series faced its own hurdles, particularly with voice acting changes that sparked fan backlash. In 2006, Pokémon USA took over dubbing duties from 4Kids Entertainment, resulting in a complete recast of the English voice cast for main characters like Ash Ketchum, which was perceived as abrupt and contributed to perceptions of declining quality during the transition. This shift marked a broader business reform, as Pokémon USA assumed in-house control of licensing and production to streamline operations amid the fading initial craze.

By 2001, the Pokémania surge had waned due to oversaturation and shifting youth interests, but the 2002 release of Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire for Game Boy Advance revitalized engagement by introducing a new region, over 100 fresh Pokémon, and double-battle mechanics, helping to sustain the franchise beyond its early peak.

#Modern Developments

The fourth generation of Pokémon games began with the release of Pokémon Diamond and Pokémon Pearl in 2006 for the Nintendo DS, introducing online trading and battling features through the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection, which allowed players worldwide to exchange Pokémon and compete remotely for the first time in the series. These titles, developed by Game Freak and published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo, expanded the franchise's connectivity, enabling global interactions that enhanced community engagement. In 2008, The Pokémon Company International was established as the U.S. branch of The Pokémon Company, responsible for managing the brand, licensing, and localization outside Asia, streamlining international operations.

The fifth generation continued on the Nintendo DS with Pokémon Black and Pokémon White in 2010, which introduced the Unova region's Pokédex containing 156 entirely new Pokémon species, excluding all previous generations to emphasize fresh storytelling and discovery. This approach, developed by Game Freak, refreshed the core gameplay by focusing on a self-contained ecosystem, while sequels Black 2 and White 2 in 2012 built upon these innovations with expanded narratives and additional Pokémon.

Transitioning to the Nintendo 3DS in 2013, Pokémon X and Pokémon Y marked the series' debut in full 3D graphics, incorporating stereoscopic visuals and new mechanics like Mega Evolution for temporary power-ups during battles. The seventh generation arrived with Pokémon Sun and Pokémon Moon in 2016, set in the Alola region and introducing regional variants—alternate forms of existing Pokémon adapted to local environments, such as the Ice/Fairy-type Alolan Vulpix. That same year, Pokémon GO, developed by Niantic in partnership with The Pokémon Company, launched as a mobile augmented reality (AR) app, encouraging real-world exploration to catch Pokémon using smartphone GPS and cameras; by 2025, it had surpassed 1 billion downloads globally.

The eighth generation shifted to the Nintendo Switch in 2019 with Pokémon Sword and Pokémon Shield, but faced significant backlash over the "Dexit" policy, where not all previous Pokémon were included in the Galar Pokédex due to development constraints on modeling and animations for over 900 species, as explained by Game Freak director Junichi Masuda. In 2022, Pokémon Legends: Arceus pioneered an open-world format in the ancient Hisui region, allowing free exploration, real-time Pokémon encounters, and action-oriented catching mechanics without traditional turn-based battles dominating gameplay. Later that year, Pokémon Scarlet and Pokémon Violet launched as the ninth generation's core titles, introducing the Terastal phenomenon—a battle mechanic where Pokémon crystallize to change their type temporarily, enhancing strategic depth and visual spectacle with Tera Types.

Generation IX expanded through the Hidden Treasure of Area Zero DLC in 2023 and 2024, adding new areas like the Kitakami highlands and Blueberry Academy, along with over 230 returning Pokémon and fresh species to address prior dex limitations.

In 2024, Pokémon Legends: Z-A was announced for a late 2025 release on Nintendo Switch, set in the Kalos region with a focus on urban redevelopment and Mega Evolutions. Additionally, 2025 releases included the life simulation game Pokémon Pokopia and a new chibi-style anime series Monpoké, further diversifying the franchise's offerings.

On the business front, Pokémon HOME debuted in 2020 as a cloud-based service for Nintendo Switch and mobile devices, enabling players to store, trade, and transfer Pokémon across compatible games in one centralized hub. In 2019, The Pokémon Company partnered with Select Button to develop Pokémon Sleep, a mobile app that tracks sleep patterns using device sensors and rewards users with Pokémon encounters based on rest quality, blending wellness trends with the franchise. Throughout the 2020s, the franchise embraced esports with official tournaments like the Pokémon Players Cup and World Championships, adapting video game competitive play to online and in-person formats amid global events.

#Media Franchise

#Video Games

The Pokémon video game series consists of mainline role-playing games (RPGs) and numerous spin-offs, primarily developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo in collaboration with The Pokémon Company. The mainline series, which forms the core of the franchise, spans nine generations released between 1996 and 2022, beginning with Pokémon Red and Green for the Game Boy in Japan. These titles follow a consistent RPG structure where players capture and train Pokémon creatures to battle trainers and gym leaders, progressing through regional adventures. The Pokémon video game series has sold over 489 million units worldwide as of March 2025, making the franchise one of the best-selling video game series in history.

Each generation introduces new Pokémon species, regions inspired by real-world locations, and gameplay refinements, such as dual-type battles in Generation II (Pokémon Gold and Silver, 1999) or the introduction of abilities and natures in Generation III (Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire, 2002). The series transitioned from handheld consoles like the Game Boy and Nintendo DS to the Nintendo 3DS and ultimately the Nintendo Switch, with Generation VIII (Pokémon Sword and Shield, 2019) marking the full shift to the latter platform. Generation IX (Pokémon Scarlet and Violet, 2022) further expanded player freedom with its semi-open world design, including expansions that added new areas and story content. Recent releases include Pokémon Legends: Z-A (2025) for the Nintendo Switch, which explores the Kalos region with a focus on urban redevelopment and has sold over 5.8 million units in its first week. Remakes of earlier titles, such as Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen (2004) for Generation III hardware, have also contributed significantly to sales, preserving classic stories with updated mechanics.

Beyond the mainline entries, spin-off games diversify the franchise across genres, including competitive battles, dungeon crawlers, and mobile experiences. Early spin-offs like Pokémon Stadium (1998) for the Nintendo 64 introduced 3D battles and stadium-style competitions using creatures from the first two generations. The Mystery Dungeon subseries, starting with Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Red Rescue Team (2005) for the Game Boy Advance, casts players as Pokémon in roguelike exploration and rescue missions. More recent mobile titles, such as Pokémon Masters EX (2019), focus on trainer-versus-trainer battles with real-time elements. These spin-offs have collectively sold tens of millions of units, broadening the franchise's appeal.

Technically, the series evolved from 2D pixel-art sprites in the initial generations to fully 3D models starting with Generation VI (Pokémon X and Y, 2013) on the Nintendo 3DS, enabling more dynamic animations and environments. Pokémon Legends: Arceus (2022) for the Nintendo Switch pioneered an open-world format, allowing seamless exploration and real-time Pokémon encounters, departing from the traditional linear progression. However, decisions like the removal of certain Pokémon from the National Pokédex in Pokémon Sword and Shield sparked fan backlash, leading to debates on completeness and accessibility.

Distribution of Pokémon games has traditionally relied on physical cartridges for handheld consoles, supplemented by digital downloads via the Nintendo eShop since the Wii era. Special events, often distributed through in-game Wi-Fi or at conventions, provide access to mythical Pokémon like Mew, enhancing collectibility without requiring purchases. By 2025, digital sales have grown substantially with the Switch's popularity, though physical editions remain prominent for collectors.

#Trading Card Game

The Pokémon Trading Card Game (TCG) is a collectible card game developed as a companion to the Pokémon video game series, where players build decks from cards representing Pokémon, Energy, and Trainers to simulate battles. It was first launched in Japan on October 20, 1996, by Media Factory, shortly after the debut of the initial Pokémon video games. The game quickly gained traction as an accessible way for fans to engage with the franchise beyond digital play, emphasizing strategy through deck construction and tactical decision-making during matches. By 2025, the TCG boasts over 18,000 unique cards, reflecting its expansive evolution and enduring appeal among collectors and competitors alike.

At its core, the TCG revolves around three primary card types: Pokémon cards, which depict creatures that serve as the main combatants and evolve through stages (Basic, Stage 1, and Stage 2); Energy cards, which provide the power needed for Pokémon attacks by attaching to them (with 11 types matching Pokémon weaknesses and resistances); and Trainer cards, which include Items for immediate effects, Supporters for once-per-turn actions, and Stadiums for ongoing field advantages. Battles occur between an Active Pokémon on each side and Benched reserves, with players taking turns to draw cards, attach Energy (once per turn), play Trainers, evolve Pokémon, and attack. A key mechanic is the Prize Card system, where each player begins with six face-down Prize Cards; knocking out an opponent's Pokémon allows the victor to claim one (or more for certain high-value cards), and the first to claim all six Prizes wins the match. These rules foster a balance of resource management and risk assessment, making the game suitable for casual and competitive play.

The TCG's card sets are released annually, often aligning with new generations of the Pokémon video games to introduce fresh Pokémon species, abilities, and mechanics. For instance, the Scarlet & Violet series debuted in March 2023, featuring over 250 cards per main expansion with innovations like the Terrain rule for shared battlefield effects and new card subtypes such as Pokémon ex. These sets are supplemented by special products like Elite Trainer Boxes and booster packs, maintaining a steady release cadence to keep the meta dynamic. Special promotional items continue to be released, including the oversized 'Pikachu at the Museum' promo card, available as a gift with purchase at the Pokémon × Natural History Museum 'Pokécology' themed pop-up store in London from January 26 to April 19, 2026, and at select UK retailers starting January 30, 2026, as well as through Pokémon Center UK with select merchandise. In 2021, The Pokémon Company International announced Pokémon TCG Live, a free-to-play digital platform that replicates the physical game's rules and allows for online battles, deck building, and code redemption for virtual cards; it entered beta testing that year and fully launched worldwide in June 2023, bridging physical and digital collecting.

Competitive play in the TCG is governed by Play! Pokémon, the official organized play program, which hosts regional, international, and World Championships events since 2004. The annual Pokémon World Championships crown masters division champions through Swiss-style tournaments and elimination brackets, drawing thousands of players globally and awarding substantial prizes, including scholarships and exclusive cards. The game's economy underscores its cultural significance, with rare cards achieving extraordinary values; for example, the 1998 Pikachu Illustrator promo card, limited to 39 copies awarded in a Japanese contest, has sold for up to $5.275 million in private transactions, highlighting the intersection of nostalgia, scarcity, and investment appeal.

As an early multimedia tie-in, the TCG played a pivotal role in amplifying the Pokémon franchise's early sales, with its 1996 Japanese launch helping propel the video games' popularity by offering tangible extensions of the collecting and battling themes. Initially partnered with Wizards of the Coast for North American distribution starting in January 1999—the same company behind Magic: The Gathering—the TCG's global rollout under this collaboration sold millions of cards and boosted overall franchise revenue before transitioning to direct management by The Pokémon Company International in 2003. This partnership not only standardized rules for international audiences but also solidified the TCG's status as a cornerstone of Pokémon's merchandising empire.

#Anime and Manga

The Pokémon anime series premiered in Japan on April 1, 1997, introducing protagonist Ash Ketchum, a young trainer embarking on a quest to become a Pokémon Master alongside his electric-type partner Pikachu. Produced by OLM, Inc., the show follows Ash's travels through diverse regions, capturing and training Pokémon while participating in gym battles and leagues. By November 2025, the series has surpassed 1,300 episodes across 28 seasons, maintaining a format of episodic adventures interspersed with overarching arcs tied to the video game generations.

Central themes in the anime emphasize friendship between trainers and Pokémon, the bonds formed during competitive battles, and personal growth through challenges like rivalries and explorations. The narrative evolved with regional arcs, such as the 2010 Best Wishes! series, which adapted the Unova region and introduced new companions like Iris and Cilan, refreshing Ash's journey with updated animation styles and story pacing. In a significant shift, the 2023 reboot Pokémon Horizons: The Series departed from Ash's storyline, centering on new protagonists Liko and Roy as they uncover mysteries involving ancient Pokémon artifacts, accompanied by changes in voice cast to align with the fresh ensemble. The second season of Horizons premiered exclusively on Netflix in the United States on February 7, 2025.

The Pokémon manga landscape began with early serializations in Shogakukan's CoroCoro Comic magazine, starting in November 1996 with titles like Pocket Monsters, which humorously depicted trainer antics in a style loosely inspired by the games. A prominent ongoing series, Pokémon Adventures (known as Pocket Monsters Special in Japan), debuted in March 1997 and has continued serialization, written by Hidenori Kusaka and illustrated by various artists including Mato. Published in English by VIZ Media since 1999, it explores alternate-universe narratives across game generations, focusing on ensemble casts of trainers tackling crises like villainous teams and legendary Pokémon encounters, with over 60 volumes released by 2025. These manga emphasize strategic battles and character-driven plots, diverging from the anime's focus on a single protagonist.

The anime and manga have achieved widespread global syndication, airing in over 160 countries and fostering a dedicated fan culture through conventions, fan art, and community events centered on character interpretations and story expansions. Reception highlights their role in popularizing themes of companionship and competition, with the anime's accessibility contributing to its longevity on platforms like Netflix and YouTube. Spin-offs such as Pokémon Chronicles, which aired from 2002 to 2003, provided side stories featuring supporting characters like Misty and Brock, further enriching the universe without relying on Ash's central arc.

#Films and Other Adaptations

The Pokémon franchise has produced 23 animated theatrical films since 1998, each serving as standalone side stories often featuring legendary Pokémon and expanding on elements from the core video games. These films, distributed in Japan by Toho, typically premiered during the summer and tie loosely to the anime series without directly advancing its main plot. The inaugural film, Pokémon: The First Movie – Mewtwo Strikes Back (1998), introduced the cloned Pokémon Mewtwo and grossed approximately $163.6 million worldwide, establishing the series' commercial viability. Subsequent entries, such as Pokémon: The Movie 2000 (1999) and Pokémon 3: The Movie (2000), continued this tradition, focusing on epic confrontations involving mythical creatures like Lugia and Entei, and collectively contributing to over $1.8 billion in global box office earnings across the franchise's films.

In live-action adaptations, Warner Bros. released Pokémon: Detective Pikachu in 2019, a film set in a live-action rendition of the Pokémon world where humans coexist with the creatures. Starring Ryan Reynolds as the voice of Detective Pikachu, the movie explored a noir-style mystery in Ryme City and achieved $433 million in worldwide box office revenue, marking the highest-grossing video game adaptation at the time of release. As of 2025, a live-action Pokémon television series remains in active development at Netflix, with Lucifer co-showrunner Joe Henderson attached to write and executive produce, though no premiere date has been announced.

Beyond cinema, the franchise has ventured into miscellaneous media, including commemorative postage stamps and stage productions. Japan Post issued its first official Pokémon stamps on July 7, 2021, featuring seasonal designs with Pokémon like Pikachu and Eevee, available in sheets priced at ¥63 and ¥84. In the United States, the U.S. Postal Service released a set of 20 spring-themed Pokémon stamps on September 19, 2023, depicting characters such as Grookey and Jigglypuff at $1.20 each. Stage adaptations include Pokémon Live!, a musical that toured the United States from late 1999 into 2000, blending live actors, puppets, and Pokémon costumes to reenact adventures from the early games and anime. Additionally, the 2021 web series Pokémon Evolutions, an eight-episode anthology produced by The Pokémon Company International, revisited key regions from the video games in reverse chronological order, offering self-contained stories that delve into trainer journeys and Pokémon bonds.

These adaptations have significantly amplified the franchise's reach, with films and related media driving cross-promotion that boosts video game sales and merchandise demand—evidenced by the overall Pokémon brand generating over $100 billion in lifetime revenue across all sectors. By introducing new narratives, such as Mewtwo's origin or urban human-Pokémon societies in Detective Pikachu, they enrich the lore beyond the games' core mechanics, fostering deeper fan engagement without altering established canon.

#Business and Organization

#Corporate Structure

The Pokémon Company was formed in 1998 as a joint venture between Nintendo (32% ownership), Game Freak (approximately 34%), and Creatures Inc. (approximately 34%), initially operating as Pokémon Center Co., Ltd. to manage the burgeoning franchise's brand and merchandise operations. By 2000, it had restructured for full oversight of the intellectual property, relocating and expanding its headquarters to the Roppongi Hills Mori Tower in Tokyo, Japan, where it coordinates global strategy and licensing.

To support international growth, Pokémon USA was established in 1999 to oversee Western market activities, including localization, marketing, and distribution; this entity evolved into The Pokémon Company International (TPCi) through a 2008 reorganization, handling operations across the Americas, Europe, Australia, and other non-Asian regions. TPCi functions as a wholly owned subsidiary of the parent company, focusing on brand management outside Asia, while dedicated regional offices in Europe (such as in London) and Asia (including subsidiaries in South Korea and Taiwan) manage localized promotions, events, and partnerships.

Leadership at The Pokémon Company centers on Tsunekazu Ishihara, who has served as president and CEO since the entity's inception in 1998, directing intellectual property oversight, cross-media coordination, and long-term franchise planning. Ishihara's role emphasizes collaborative governance among the joint owners, ensuring unified decision-making on content development and global expansion. Creatures Inc., as a co-owner and integral partner, specializes in the Pokémon Trading Card Game's design and production, leveraging its expertise in card mechanics and digital adaptations without formal mergers but through sustained joint ventures.

In 2025, The Pokémon Company expanded its technology divisions to bolster mobile app development, including initiatives like the Pokémon Events app for event management and enhancements to digital TCG platforms, driving innovation in user engagement and augmented reality features. These efforts have contributed to the franchise's cumulative revenue exceeding $147 billion as of 2024, underscoring its position as the highest-grossing media property.

#Merchandising and Licensing

The expansion of the Pokémon franchise into merchandising began in the mid-1990s, shortly after the release of the initial video games, with early efforts coordinated by Creatures Inc. to develop toys and apparel. In Japan, Bandai served as the primary licensing partner, producing the first official Pokémon toys, such as the Bandai Club series, starting in May 1996, and handling trading cards through Carddass vending machines from September 1996. In the United States, Hasbro secured the licensing rights for toys and apparel in 1998, releasing products like action figures and collectibles through 2000, before the license transitioned to other partners. The establishment of The Pokémon Company in April 1998 centralized oversight of these licensing activities, ensuring coordinated global expansion of consumer products.

By 2025, the franchise encompassed a vast array of licensed merchandise, ranging from plush toys and clothing to mobile apps and collectibles. Revenue from these licensing deals forms a core economic pillar, exemplified by the 1999 partnership with McDonald's for Pokémon-themed Happy Meals, which introduced promotional toys and cards to millions of consumers and marked one of the earliest major cross-promotions.

Key licensing agreements have further diversified the product landscape, including a long-term partnership with Universal Studios Japan announced in October 2021 to develop interactive Pokémon attractions, which debuted in March 2023 and integrated themed rides, shows, and merchandise within the park. Another notable collaboration occurred in 2023 with the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, celebrating the museum's 50th anniversary through Pokémon-inspired artwork on items like trading card playmats, pins, and apparel, blending the franchise's characters with Van Gogh's paintings. In January 2026, The Pokémon Company announced a collaboration with the Natural History Museum in London for a 'Pokécology' themed pop-up store in the Cranbourne Boutique shop, running from January 26 to April 19, 2026, featuring exclusive merchandise inspired by the museum's collections and Pokémon ecology, along with an oversized Pokémon TCG promo card featuring 'Pikachu at the Museum' available as a gift with purchase at the pop-up and select UK retailers starting January 30, 2026. In November 2025, The Pokémon Company announced PokéPark KANTO, a permanent theme park in Tokyo set to open in February 2026, featuring over 600 Pokémon encounters and expanding theme park merchandising. The Pokémon Company has also ventured into digital merchandising, conducting experiments with NFTs in 2021 through third-party platforms tokenizing collectible cards, though official digital collectibles, such as blockchain-based souvenirs, expanded more substantially in subsequent years.

Merchandise and licensing account for approximately 70% of the franchise's overall revenue, providing essential financial stability that extends beyond core video game sales and supports ongoing development across media. In 2023, licensed products alone generated $10.8 billion in global retail sales, underscoring their role in sustaining the brand's longevity and cultural relevance under The Pokémon Company's management.

#Cultural Impact

#Pokémania Phenomenon

The Pokémania phenomenon, peaking in 1999-2000, marked an explosive surge in Pokémon's popularity following its North American debut in 1998, driven by the interplay of video games, the animated series, and especially the trading card game. In the United States, media coverage amplified the frenzy, with widespread reports of children trading cards obsessively during school hours, leading to disruptions in classrooms and playgrounds across states like Massachusetts, New York, New Jersey, Washington, and New Hampshire. Pikachu emerged as the franchise's breakout pop culture icon, its lightning-bolt-tailed design adorning merchandise and symbolizing the "gotta catch 'em all" ethos that captivated young audiences. This hype contributed to an economic boom, with Pokémon generating approximately $700 million in U.S. retail sales in 1999 alone, encompassing games, cards, and toys.

Societal reactions were polarized, with parental concerns centering on the addictive nature of card collecting and trading, which mirrored gambling behaviors and led to excessive spending—some children reportedly amassing debts of up to $2,000 in six months. Schools responded aggressively, implementing bans and confiscating cards to curb distractions, with teachers instructed to return them only at the end of the day to restore focus on learning. The international expansion into markets like Europe and Latin America further fueled the mania, as global demand strained supply chains and intensified the cross-cultural excitement.

Controversies escalated amid the hype, particularly regarding health risks amplified by the 1997 Japanese broadcast of episode 38, "Dennō Senshi Porygon," which triggered photosensitive epileptic seizures in approximately 685 viewers—mostly children—due to rapid red-and-blue flashing lights at 12 Hz, hospitalizing hundreds and affecting up to 12,000 with symptoms like dizziness and convulsions. In the U.S., this incident prompted amplified epilepsy warnings for the animated series upon its 1999 premiere, with disclaimers added to episodes and broadcasts to alert photosensitive viewers. Legal backlash included a 1999 class-action lawsuit filed in San Diego Federal District Court against Nintendo and partners, alleging the trading cards promoted illegal gambling through low odds (1 in 33 for premium holographics) and addictive pack-opening mechanics, with rare cards reselling for up to $50 and fostering cutthroat trading among children.

By 2001, the mania waned due to market saturation, as overproduction flooded the trading card sector, causing drastic price collapses for rare cards and wiping out values for young collectors, prompting layoffs at Wizards of the Coast. The shift toward new game generations, including preparations for Generation III, diluted focus on the original 151 Pokémon, signaling a transition from widespread craze to more sustained, niche enthusiasm.

#Global Legacy and Influences

Pokémon has profoundly shaped the gaming industry by popularizing the creature-collection genre, where players capture, train, and battle fantastical monsters, inspiring numerous titles including Digimon, which emerged as a direct competitor in the late 1990s with its digital monster-rearing mechanics. This influence extends to modern games like Temtem, an MMORPG explicitly designed as a creature-collection adventure that incorporates multiplayer elements while echoing Pokémon's core loop of taming and evolving beings. Beyond gaming, Pokémon icons such as Pikachu have permeated global pop culture, symbolizing Japanese soft power and engaging international audiences through various promotions and events.

Economically, Pokémon stands as the highest-grossing media franchise in history, surpassing other giants like Star Wars and Mario through its transmedia empire model, integrating diverse revenue streams across digital and physical products to sustain long-term profitability and global market dominance. This success has set a blueprint for other franchises, demonstrating how interconnected media ecosystems can drive consumer engagement.

The franchise's inspirations have led to both positive adaptations and critiques; educators have leveraged Pokémon's ecosystem of over 1,000 species to teach biodiversity and ecological interactions, with studies showing improved student engagement and understanding of real-world biology through game-based analogies. However, it has faced criticism for promoting consumerism, as the "gotta catch 'em all" mantra encourages endless collecting of merchandise and digital items, mirroring broader societal pressures around acquisition and status.

In 2025, Pokémon maintains modern relevance through expanding esports, with the Pokémon World Championships in Anaheim setting attendance records and announcing enhanced online tournaments to broaden global participation. Diversity initiatives, including The Pokémon Company's inclusion policies and gender-balanced character designs in recent games like Scarlet and Violet, foster equitable representation among trainers and fans. Vibrant global fan communities, from in-person events like Community Day celebrations in over 190 countries to online forums and content creator gatherings at Worlds, continue to build a supportive network that evolves with the franchise. The enduring popularity traces back to the initial Pokémania craze, which laid the foundation for this sustained worldwide phenomenon.
